materials.text: Gardens, storage, house construction, hunting and trade supported a settled river community.

citations.locator: Women’s Influence, Processing Foods and Food Storage

knowledge.text: Women’s ownership, clan cooperation and skilled supervision were part of earthlodge life.

custody.text: Depressions and community accounts explain village history; the standing interpretive lodge is reconstructed.

name: Hidatsa villages: gardens, earthlodges and exchange
place: Big Hidatsa Village and the Knife–Missouri river confluence, North Dakota
geographicPrecision: Locator for a selected Hidatsa village landscape; neighboring Mandan and Arikara histories remain distinct. The displayed earthlodge is a modern reconstruction.

interval.label: Big Hidatsa village occupation, c. 1600–1845
interval.note: NPS’s selected village frame. 1845 marks relocation to Like-a-Fishhook, not the end of Hidatsa people, gardening or earthlodge knowledge. Other Knife River villages have their own different starting dates.

question: What changes when women’s gardens and houses are placed at the center of Plains history?
summary: Women’s gardens, houses and food stores helped make Hidatsa villages places of household work and regional exchange. Cultivation joined hunting and gathering rather than replacing them. Community-authored teaching and a named woman’s later recollections explain knowledge and authority while distinguishing Big Hidatsa from subsequent homes, displacement and continuing life.

sections.title: Gardens produced food and possibilities for exchange
sections.text: The community-authored NPS guide places women’s cultivation at the center of village economic life. Preparing land, tending corn, beans, squash and sunflowers, then drying and storing food required a connected sequence of work. Stored crops could sustain a household beyond harvest and supply exchange with visitors. Hunting and gathering also contributed to the food base. A village was therefore more than a cluster of buildings: fields, drying spaces and storage linked its residents to the surrounding land and other communities.

citations.locator: Teacher’s Note; Women’s Influence; Processing Foods; Food Storage;Hunting and Foraging

sections.title: An earthlodge joined construction with household authority
sections.text: NPS describes women constructing, owning and maintaining earthlodges through clan cooperation and experienced supervision. Gathering building material and making a supporting framework were practical tasks connected with knowledge and responsibility. Drying racks and cache pits extended this work into food storage. The standing interpretive lodge helps explain a structure, while shallow depressions mark former houses at Big Hidatsa. These are different forms of evidence. Neither the modern building nor the tool illustration establishes every historical resident, tool maker or ownership arrangement by appearance alone.

citations.locator: Construction/ownership; clan cooperation; depressions and reconstruction

sections.title: The river brought visitors and changing pressures
sections.text: River travel helped make the villages places of exchange. Goods, visitors and disease moved through these relationships; the NPS historical account connects the 1837 smallpox epidemic with a steamboat arrival. MHA’s history describes village survivors consolidating and the 1845 move to Like-a-Fishhook. Such changes altered residence and community organization. The Big Hidatsa occupation frame ends at that move, not at the end of a people. The different Mandan, Hidatsa and Arikara histories should be read together without erasing their distinctions.

citations.locator: Three Affiliated Tribes;The Hidatsa Proper;Village & Relocations

sections.title: Later voices explain continuity through changed settings
sections.text: Maxi´diwiac, also known as Buffalobird-woman, describes garden boundaries, permission to use adjoining ground and letting fields rest in an account published in 1917. Her memories concern Like-a-Fishhook, after the selected Big Hidatsa occupation. They add a particular woman’s knowledge rather than a timeless rule for all earlier villages. Twentieth-century government projects brought further displacement. MHA’s account describes families moved from fertile bottomlands as the Garrison Dam transformed their landscape. That later history belongs to the separate reference, alongside the knowledge and communities that continued.

returnPrompt: Compare this farming village with a communal bison-hunting landscape. Name a real difference, a shared need for knowledge and a limit in the evidence.

deeperReading.title: A named account still has an interpreter and editor
deeperReading.text: Wilson’s foreword describes recording Maxi´diwiac’s account through Edward Goodbird’s translation in 1912 and reading earlier notes back for corrections during later visits. He also explains arranging the material and its English idiom. This makes authorship and mediation part of the evidence. The account is not an unedited sound recording. Nor should Wilson’s ambition to recover an unchanged earlier culture become our conclusion. A woman’s detailed recollection can preserve decisions, relationships and expertise without representing every person or directly describing the 1600 village.

deeperReading.title: Field knowledge includes boundaries and limits of memory
deeperReading.text: In her account, adjoining gardeners shared work along a boundary and sought permission before planting it. She describes resting fields flexibly, rather than following one fixed timetable. Her explanation of a garden map also names its limits: approximate positions and fields near her own family, not every garden. These statements help us ask how knowledge and use of land were negotiated. They do not create a measured survey of Big Hidatsa. The book also describes Goodbird making a model hoe under her direction from a steer shoulder blade. That identified model must not be silently equated with the separate NPS tool illustration. The modern lodge photograph and teaching-tool illustration have different limits again: they explain structures and materials without becoming dated household artifacts. A fuller account needs more women’s and families’ histories, source-specific plans and the circumstances of each later relocation.

evidenceReading.title: Garden work, a mediated voice and different place histories
evidenceReading.introduction: The supplied images are a modern reconstruction and teaching illustration. Community-authored text and a later named recollection add evidence of work and authority that image form alone cannot recover.

items.label: A teaching tool is not an accessioned ancient implement
items.text: The NPS guide identifies a shoulder-blade hoe and digging stick, and describes women’s work producing crops for use and trade.
items.interpretation: Read materials and form with the account of work. The illustration does not supply a particular maker, exact production date, findspot or an unchanged division of labor for every household.

citations.locator: Teacher’s Note; Women’s Influence; tool illustration

items.label: A named woman describes permission and adaptable practice
items.text: Maxi´diwiac’s later recollections describe neighbors’ garden boundaries, permission and flexible periods of resting fields.
items.interpretation: These are particular remembered arrangements, mediated through translation and editing. They should not become a timeless land law or direct evidence for every Big Hidatsa garden before 1845.

items.label: Relocation changes the setting without ending the people
items.text: Big Hidatsa’s selected occupation ends in 1845. MHA separately describes Like-a-Fishhook and the later Garrison Dam relocations.
items.interpretation: An occupation endpoint, a dam-construction milestone and household relocation are different changes. Keeping their dates separate prevents a vanished-people story and preserves the work of continuity.

familyActivity.title: Explain a tool with a source
steps: Look at the teaching illustration. Identify its animal and plant materials from the supplied explanation.
Read the capsule and connect one illustrated tool with preparing soil. Name another task in the sequence of growing and storing food.
Separate what the image shows from what the community account says about work.
Write one supported claim and one question requiring a dated tool, household account or another source. Do not infer a universal rule from shape alone.
familyActivity.explanation: Source capsule — editorial paraphrase: The image illustrates a hoe with a bison shoulder blade attached to wood and a separate wooden digging stick. It is a teaching illustration, not a dated excavated tool photograph. The community-authored NPS guide describes women preparing soil, growing corn, beans, squash and sunflowers, drying crops and storing food. The image helps explain materials and form; the supplied account explains work and authority that shape alone cannot establish. Describe one supported connection between material, tool and garden work, then identify the additional evidence needed to explain a particular household.

review.reviewer: Codex selected source consultation and internal author QA; not independent MHA/community or historian acceptance
review.scope: Women’s cultivation, household construction/storage, exchange and changing settings through renewed community/NPS accounts and a selected mediated named recollection. Two new substantive source records and four dated renewals preserve prior scopes. The complete original 1600–1845 interval/note/claims/dimensions/terms and all old media fields/pixels remain exact. No media object, annotation, placeStudy, route or relationship is added.
limitations: The 1917 account presents later Like-a-Fishhook memories through Goodbird’s translation and Wilson’s editing. Selected text/edition metadata, not the complete facsimile, was consulted. Original manuscript/audio and the complete 1987 annotated reissue were not read; LOC direct access returned 403 and its catalogue description is indexed evidence only.

Wilson’s unchanged-culture/representative-person/pre-Columbian projections are not adopted. The NPS teaching guide and MHA webpage also contain broad or inherited outsider passages; no extinction language, population total, universal household experience or harmonized contradictory date is adopted.

Different source dates remain separate: c.1600–1845 Big Hidatsa; later Like-a-Fishhook recollections and 1917 publication;1953 dam completion in NPS and fall 1954 relocation completion in MHA. No law/treaty, dam-compensation or demographic claim is independently certified.

No village-plan media is included by this module. The identified Lower Hidatsa plan concerns a different occupation and lacks established creator/creation-date/image ownership in its page description. A remembered Like-a-Fishhook garden map is a separate potential source, not a measured Big Hidatsa survey. Any visual adoption requires its own inspected pixels, rights and date/geometry proposal.

Both existing images were actually viewed and all four files hashed. Exposure/creation dates remain unknown where the original records say unknown. The standing lodge is a reconstruction and the tool image explanatory; no new rights, artwork source or ancient findspot is inferred.

Public introductory accounts do not grant permission to reproduce restricted songs, stories, sacred rights or ceremonies. None is copied or reenacted. Independent historical/community review, family usability, screen-reader/device behavior and physical print acceptance remain open.
